odo_pennywhistle.name: Odo Pennywhistle
odo_pennywhistle.personality: chirpy, canny, never quite telling where he got things
odo_pennywhistle.voice: market patter, sales pitches, and weather he has just walked through
greet: Ah, a customer with sensible boots! Come, come. Today's wares are tomorrow's regrets.
Back already? Good. I rather hoped the road would bring you my way.
Odo Pennywhistle, at your service, and at your price. Mind the lantern.
Rain in the east, sun in the west, and a good bargain right here. Look about!
You again. I keep a shelf for people who come twice. It has better stock.
Ha! The lamp-bearer. I thought I felt a draught of destiny. Buy something.
Quick, before the other customers arrive. There are none. But quick anyway.
Fresh from a place I will not name, to a customer I am delighted to name. Hello!
bye: Fair winds and full pockets. Find me again, if the days allow.
Mind the road. And if you see me somewhere odd, that is simply where I am.
Pleasure doing business. I will pretend I did not enjoy it.
Off with you, then. Come back on a day that ends in a vowel.

say: Hold still, hold still, you strike me as a person who has never been sold something rare. A tragedy, and I am the cure.
Odo Pennywhistle. I walk the roads on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays. Don't ask what I do the other days. I would only lie, and badly.
Everything I carry was made to be a little more than it looks. Buy what suits you. I have only one of each, so you cannot say I did not warn you.

lines.text: Tuesdays, Thursdays, Sundays. I do not keep a diary. The sun tells me where to be.
One of each, always. The second one has a way of disappearing from my cart.
Where do I get my stock? A gentleman never tells. A merchant never remembers.
My cart has seven wheels. Don't count them. I have a superstition about being counted.
A coat with a charm in the lining sells itself. A coat without one needs me to talk, and I am tired.
There is no such thing as a bad bargain. There is only a bargain that has not found its person.
A fighter! I keep my sturdiest pieces for fighters. They bleed less, and so does my conscience.
A mage! Mind the staves. I once sold one that hummed. It haunted me for a week, and the buyer for longer.
A scout. You have the walk of a customer who counts the exits. I respect that, and price accordingly.
A healer. You will want the elixir. Everyone who wants the elixir wants it too late.
Weather today: unreliable. Roads today: worse. Prices today: honest, in the sense that I have never lied about them.
I once sold a dragon's tooth to a man who wanted a toothpick. We both went home happy.
People ask if my goods are cursed. A little, sometimes. But only the good kind of cursed, like a tune you cannot forget.
That glow in your palm. May I look? No? A pity. I would have paid nearly anything.
I have a cousin in the south who sells sand. Everyone laughs. He is richer than I am.
Gold rattles. Silver sings. Copper only complains, and I do not stock complaints.
I never sell the same thing twice to the same buyer. A matter of pride, and of the cart's limited volume.
The road remembers the people who walk it. I try to be forgettable, so it forgets me quickly.
Brinewick. Salt on the wind and a harbour that pretends to be calm. I bought a very good net there once.
Goblins camped by the ford were bad for trade. I charged them double and they paid in ears.
Lanternmoor has stopped lighting its mine. I stopped selling it candles. I felt dreadful, but I did not give them away.
The spiders below Lanternmoor are gone? Then the miners will want boots. I am out of boots. I will fetch boots.
Gallowkeep is quiet, they say. I crossed the ridge at dawn and the wind was only wind. I almost missed the orcs.
Hask, dead? He owed me for six crates of rope. I will send the bill to the chapel. Someone must have kept it.
